title: Take the make-ready print and the joint-use record
instruction: Read who owns which space on this pole, what the make-ready called for, and what the sag and clearance over the road are meant to be.
rationale: A joint-use pole is shared property with a written allocation: the electric utility's supply conductors at the top, the communications space below, and a separation between them that the National Electrical Safety Code sets and the make-ready engineering recorded span by span. The print is what tells you which of those spaces you are allowed in and what the crossing was designed to be before you hang anything else on it.

title: Set the traffic control before anything goes up
instruction: Carry the cones out and run the taper upstream of the truck, working with your back to the traffic side.
rationale: The taper comes first, before the outriggers and long before the boom. A crew that sets up and then closes the lane spends the whole set-up standing in live traffic, which is exactly the part of this job that kills people. The taper is also what the driver reads — it is the warning, not the cones around the truck.

title: Sound and inspect the pole before it takes a load change
instruction: Hammer from the groundline up, listening for the ring going dull, and hold while you work round the pole.
rationale: A wood pole rots from the inside out at the groundline, where the sound one rings and the hollow one thuds. This pole is about to take a new cable, a new pull and a lift working off it, and a load change is exactly what finds a shell-rotten pole. A pole you would not climb is a pole you do not add a span to either.

title: Set the lift up on the roadway
instruction: Brake, chocks, then both outriggers down onto pads — kerb side first, traffic side last.
rationale: The ANSI A92 aerial device standards treat the chassis as part of the machine: an aerial device worked off a truck that can roll or settle is a different machine from the one that was rated. Brake and chocks before outriggers, because outriggers set on a truck that is still free to move take the load and then lose it. Traffic side last so the time you spend in the lane is the shortest it can be.

title: Mark the supply space and agree the limit
instruction: Mark the boundary of the space you will not go above, and say it out loud to the ground worker before the boom moves.
rationale: The limit is agreed on the ground, in daylight, by two people, and not judged from a bucket by one. Everything above that mark belongs to the electric utility and needs a qualified line worker; everything below it is yours. Naming it out loud is what makes it something the ground worker can call you on when the boom starts creeping up toward it.

title: Bond the strand at the pole
instruction: Clean the strand, get the clamp on bare metal and hold it while the bond is made up to the pole ground.
rationale: The messenger is a grounded conductor and the bond is what makes the entire span, the pole ground and the utility's grounded conductor into a single potential. It is the difference between a strand that stays at earth and a strand that sits between two potentials for the length of the block. It is also what carries fault current away from the person holding a lashing machine on it.

title: Prove the bond, do not assume it
instruction: Read the bond across the strand and the pole ground, and commit on the resistance.
rationale: A clamp that looks right on a galvanised strand can be sitting on zinc oxide and reading open. The reason to measure is that a bad bond and a good bond are visually identical, and the span you are about to clamp a cable to is either grounded for a thousand feet or it is not.

title: Swing the boom up to the strand and keep it clear
instruction: Bring the bucket up to the communications space and hold the clearance steady the whole way through the swing.
rationale: Clearance is not a position, it is the whole arc. The boom passes through everything between where it started and where it stops, and the tightest point is almost never where the bucket ends up. Swing in too far and you are into the supply space you are not qualified for; swing out too far and the bucket and everything in it is hanging over the open travelled lane instead of the closed one.

title: Get the cable up onto the strand
instruction: Take the cable end up on the hand line and clamp it into the strand at the pole.
rationale: The cable is carried to the strand rather than pulled along the ground, because a fibre cable dragged over a kerb and a driveway arrives with the sheath opened and the buffer tubes crushed, and none of that shows up until the span is up and the OTDR says so. The pole end is clamped first so the lasher has something to pull against.

title: Set the reel payoff under tension control
instruction: Set the payoff brake and commit when the running tension sits where the make-ready sag calls for.
rationale: The reel is what decides the tension in the span, and tension decides the sag, and sag is what the road crossing clearance was calculated from. Too loose and the cable is on the ground behind you; too tight and you overhaul the strand, lift the crossing and load poles and guys in a direction the make-ready never checked.

title: Run the lasher out across the span
instruction: Hold the pull steady and let the lasher ride the strand out to midspan while the reel pays off behind it.
rationale: The lasher rides the strand and wraps the cable to it as it goes, at a rate the reel can feed. Snatch it and the lashing wire breaks or the reel overhauls; stall it and you get a bare run with the cable sitting on the strand unattached. Everything it does happens out at midspan, above the road, where nobody can reach it once it is going.

title: Make up the lashing clamps at the pole
instruction: Tighten the clamps that terminate the lashing wire either side of the pole.
rationale: The lashing wire is only as good as what holds its ends. An unterminated lashing run unwinds from the end, slowly, over a season of wind, and hands you a cable hanging off a strand at midspan over a road. The clamps are the reason the span stays a span.

title: Stow the boom before anything else
instruction: Bring the bucket down, cradle the boom and get everything out of the travelled way.
rationale: The boom comes down before the paperwork, before the tools and before the cones. A stowed boom is the point at which the job stops being something a passing vehicle can turn into a fatality, and every minute between finishing the work and stowing is a minute spent in the air for no reason at all.

title: Walk the span before the lane goes back
instruction: Look up at the crossing, look down the pole at the ground, and click what has to be fixed before traffic comes back.
rationale: The last look is the only part of this job done with the cable in its final condition and the lane still yours. After the cones come in, anything you find here needs the road closed all over again, so it will not get found — it will get reported by somebody else, months later, as damage.

situation: A secondary service drop has been re-run since the make-ready and now crosses the arc your boom is swinging through, low, with a taped splice in it.
instruction: Something belonging to the power company is in the space you are turning the boom through.
missed: You kept swinging and took the drop on the boom. A taped splice in a secondary is not insulation, the fibreglass upper boom is only as good as the last dielectric test and the dirt on it, and the first anyone knows about that is the truck body going to potential with a ground worker's hand on it.

situation: A car has come through the taper, flattened the second cone and stopped in the closed lane directly beneath the bucket, with the driver looking up at you.
instruction: The lane you closed is not closed any more.
missed: You carried on lashing over an open lane with a car under you. The next vehicle through the gap did not stop, and the crew found out which of the two possible outcomes they had — something dropped from the bucket onto a moving car, or a moving car into the outriggers of a truck with someone forty feet up on it.

explanation: You went up into the supply space to move the service drop out of your way. Above the communications space the pole belongs to the electric utility and so does everything on it, and a communications worker is not a qualified employee there — not because of a demarcation agreement, but because nothing in a cable placer's training or tools is built for an energized primary. That drop gets moved by a qualified line worker, and until they arrive the job stops.

You wound the reel tension up to pull the sag out of the span. Sag is not slack to be tidied away: it is the designed condition the make-ready calculated the poles, the guys and the road crossing against. Over-tension the pull and you overhaul the strand, lift the crossing out of the profile the make-ready allowed, and load the poles in a direction nobody checked — and a wood pole carrying an unbalanced pull its guying does not answer fails at the groundline, which is also the part of it you cannot see.

You worked with the travelled lane open under the bucket. Outside-plant crews are not killed by poles, they are killed by traffic: struck by a vehicle, or dropped on when a vehicle hits the lift. The lane closure is not a courtesy to the crew, it is the only thing standing between a moving vehicle and a truck with someone in the air on top of it.

You lashed the cable onto a strand whose bond you had not proved. The bond is what ties the messenger, the pole ground and the utility's grounded conductor into one potential across the whole span. Open it and the strand stops being grounded steel and becomes a long conductor between two different potentials — which is what you are about to clamp a cable and a lashing machine to, by hand, from a bucket.

title: Read the method of procedure
instruction: Check which string failed, the plant voltage, the breaker, and the torque figures.
rationale: The MOP is what turns this from a guess into a job: it names the exact string that failed, the breaker that isolates it, and the torque figure the manufacturer publishes for that link, on a plant that never goes fully dark for the job. Working from memory on a live −48 V plant is how a tech opens the breaker feeding the site instead of the one feeding the dead string.

title: Ventilate the cabinet and check for hydrogen
instruction: Start the cabinet fan, open the door, and read the hydrogen monitor before any tool goes in.
rationale: Every cell on charge is off-gassing hydrogen continuously, not just when it is being worked on, and a cabinet that has been closed up for a week can hold enough of it that a single tool spark is all it takes to ignite the head-space above the strings. The fan runs and the monitor reads below the limit before a screwdriver, let alone a wrench, goes anywhere near a terminal.

title: Face shield, insulated gloves, jewellery off
instruction: Shield for acid and arc, gloves for the terminals, ring and watch in the pocket.
rationale: A short across a stationary battery is not a quiet event — it is a flash and a spray of electrolyte from a cell that can push several hundred amps into whatever bridges its posts. The shield and the insulated gloves are sized for exactly that failure, and the ring comes off first because a wedding band across two terminals does not need a dropped tool to complete the circuit — a hand resting the wrong way is enough.

title: Isolate the failed string
instruction: Open string 1's breaker and confirm the plant is carrying the load on string 2 and the rectifiers.
rationale: Opening the string's own breaker is what actually takes it off the bus rather than merely disconnecting the tech's attention from it — the plant keeps running the whole time on the rectifiers and string 2, which is the entire point of a dual-string design. Skip the breaker and every terminal on the failed string is still riding the same −48 V the site depends on.

title: Verify the string is off the bus
instruction: Read across the string breaker's load side and commit once it shows the string isolated.
rationale: An open breaker handle is a claim about the world, not a measurement of it — a welded contact, a mislabeled panel, or a breaker thrown on the wrong string all look identical from the front of the cabinet. The meter reading across the load side is what actually tells a tech whether the terminals about to be touched are riding the bus voltage or sitting at zero.

title: Cover the adjacent terminals
instruction: Insulating covers on every terminal you are not working on.
rationale: An insulated wrench only protects the two posts it is actually touching, and a live cabinet has a dozen more within reach of a hand or an elbow bracing against the rack. Covering every terminal but the one currently in hand is what keeps an ordinary slip a non-event instead of the moment a socket or a forearm bridges two live posts on the string next door.

title: Fit the replacement battery
instruction: Carry the new battery from the cart and set it in the string's empty position.
rationale: A stationary battery string only floats correctly when every cell in it is the same model at the same state, in the same orientation the manufacturer specified — the replacement goes into the exact bay the failed cell came out of, terminals facing the bus, checked against the position twice before a single intercell link is torqued down onto it.

title: Torque the intercell links
instruction: Insulated torque wrench on each link, one hand, hold to the click.
rationale: An under-torqued link is a loose connection that heats under load until it eventually fails open on the busiest night of the year, and an over-torqued one cracks the post it is clamped to, which fails in exactly the same way but sooner. The manufacturer's figure, an insulated wrench, and one hand kept clear of every other terminal is what makes this a routine step instead of the moment that creates the next outage.

title: Check the string cell by cell
instruction: Read each cell's voltage on the new string and commit inside the float band.
rationale: A string is only as good as its weakest cell — one reading low drags the whole string's capacity down with it, and one reading high is already cooking itself toward the failure that put the last cell in this same bay. Every cell on the new string reads inside the float band before anyone trusts it to sit on the bus next to a string that has been floating there for years.

title: Return the string to the bus
instruction: Close string 1's breaker and confirm both strings share the load.
rationale: Closing the breaker only returns the string to the bus; it does not by itself prove the two strings are actually sharing the load the way a healthy plant should. That gets confirmed at the plant controller before the cabinet doors close, because a string that closes onto the bus but never picks up its share is a failure the site will not notice until the other string is asked to carry all of it alone.

title: Walk the plant before closing up
instruction: Inspect the other string and the bus before the cabinet closes; click what needs the next MOP.
rationale: The site is up right now on string 2, and a corroded post that reads fine under float voltage today is exactly the connection that opens under load the next time the rectifiers drop out and the plant needs everything that string can give. Whether the site survives that outage depends on whether somebody wrote up the sulfate crust on the way out or left it for the next crew to find the hard way.

situation: The cabinet door has swung most of the way shut behind you while both hands are on the torque wrench, and the H₂ reading you cleared ten minutes ago is climbing back into the amber.
instruction: The cabinet's closing up on you.
missed: The door stayed most of the way shut through the whole torque sequence with hydrogen climbing behind it. Nothing sparked this time, but an insulated wrench slipping half an inch onto a bare post in that cabinet would have had exactly the ignition source the ventilation step exists to keep away from that gas.

situation: With the new cell seated but its intercell links not yet made up, the plant controller flags a few tenths of a volt on string 1's isolated side — a shared load lead nobody accounted for may be back-feeding it.
instruction: String 1 isn't reading dead anymore.
missed: The links went on with the isolation only assumed, not reread. A few stray volts across two posts under a torque wrench is a small number until the wrench bridges them, and by then it is exactly the same short a fully live string would have produced.

explanation: You picked up the uninsulated wrench. Across two battery terminals it is a dead short with hundreds of amps behind it — it welds itself to the posts and sprays molten metal at your face. Insulated tools, and one hand at a time.
You used the cordless drill inside the unventilated cabinet. Charging batteries make hydrogen; the cabinet is ventilated and checked before a tool that can spark goes inside it.
You went at the terminals with your ring on. Metal jewellery across a terminal is a short that does not come off; it goes in your pocket before the cabinet opens.
You started on string 2 — the live string still feeding the bus. The failed string is isolated at its breaker and identified before a terminal is touched; the other string is what keeps the site up.

title: Take the energised electrical work permit
instruction: Read why this cannot be de-energised, the incident energy, and the approach boundaries.
rationale: Everything in this hall is fed twice so that no single feed ever has to be someone's emergency. The permit is where the justification for working it live is written down and signed, and it carries the incident energy the PPE is chosen against.

title: Arc PPE to the permit's category, and the boundary
instruction: Hood and gloves to the stated category, boundary tape before anyone else walks the aisle.
rationale: The boundary is as much for the technician walking past with an armful of drives as for you. In a hot aisle nobody expects an energised worker, because normally there isn't one.

title: Prove which side you are on
instruction: Meter on the B-side tap point, live-dead-live, and commit on the reading.
rationale: A and B run parallel, a metre apart, in identical housings, with the labels facing whichever way the installer felt like. The meter is the only thing in this hall that actually knows which one is which.

title: Lock and tag the B-side feeder
instruction: Your lock on the B-side breaker upstream, tag with the permit number.
rationale: The side you are working is off and stays off because your lock is on it. Without that, the only thing between you and a re-energised busway is the fact that nobody happened to want it back yet.

title: Lift the floor tile and barrier the hole
instruction: Puller on the tile, lift it out, and set the barrier round the opening.
rationale: The tap-off's whip drops into the floor void to the cabinet. The tile comes up, and the hole gets a barrier immediately — not when you remember, because you will be looking up for the next twenty minutes.

title: Break down the packaging outside the hall
instruction: Box, bag and pallet go on the cart and out — nothing with fibre on it crosses the threshold.
rationale: The hall's air handlers pull everything that sheds into the containment and then through fifty thousand pounds of server. Cardboard is not untidy in here, it is contamination.

title: Lift the tap-off box to the busway
instruction: Two people, or the lift — the box goes up square to the plug-in opening.
rationale: A tap-off box is thirty kilos held overhead at arm's length. Square to the opening or it will not seat, and a box hanging half-engaged off a live busway run is the worst place in the hall to be standing.

title: Stab the tap-off home
instruction: Steady pressure, straight in, and hold until the interlock latches.
rationale: The stabs have to engage together. Rocking it in engages one phase before the others, which is a phase-to-phase fault inside a box you are holding. Straight in, held, until the mechanical interlock says it is home.

title: Torque the tap-off terminations
instruction: Each lug to the figure on the label, and commit inside the band.
rationale: Under-torqued lugs are the single most common cause of failures in this equipment: they run hot, oxidise, run hotter, and fail as an arcing fault months later with the hall on them.

title: Close the B-side feeder
instruction: Lock off, permit closed, and close the breaker to re-energise the side.
rationale: The side comes back on when the work is finished and the permit is closed, in that order. The hall has been running on one side for the whole job, which is the point of building it that way — and also why finishing matters.

title: Thermal-scan the terminations under load
instruction: Scan each lug once the load is on and commit inside the temperature band.
rationale: Torque is a proxy; temperature is the measurement. A joint that reads twenty degrees over its neighbours under load is a bad joint regardless of what the wrench said, and it is found now or it is found by the fire alarm.

title: Walk the aisle before you sign off
instruction: Look over the containment, the whips and the tiles before the barrier comes down; click what needs a ticket.
rationale: In a hall where nothing can be switched off, the things that take a floor down are almost never the work anyone planned. They are the loose ends left behind by work that went fine.

situation: The busway above you is labelled B-SIDE. The breaker you have just locked is tagged A-FEED on the panel schedule.
instruction: Two labels, and they disagree.
missed: You carried on with the contradiction unresolved. It happened to be the B-side. The label that was wrong is still wrong, and the next person will read it the same way you nearly did.

situation: Somebody has moved your barrier to get a cart past. The floor tile is still out and the hole is open in the aisle behind you.
instruction: There is an open floor void behind you and your hands are full.
missed: The hole stayed open and unbarriered for the rest of the job. Nobody went into it. That was luck and traffic, not control — and the cart that moved your barrier came back the other way.

explanation: That is the A-side busway — the live one carrying the floor. Concurrent maintainability means one side is always energised so the hall never goes down; it also means the energised side is always an arm's length from the one you are working on, and the only thing telling them apart is the label and the meter.
You brought packaging into the hall. Cardboard and pallets shed fibre straight into the air handlers and the containment, which is why they are broken down at the dock and never cross the threshold.

You started work on energised equipment without the permit. An energised electrical work permit is not paperwork for its own sake — it is the document where somebody senior had to write down why this cannot be done de-energised, and sign their name to that.

You left the raised-floor tile out behind you with no barrier. A missing tile in a dark hot aisle is a broken ankle for the next person through, and the tile puller is sitting in the hole where nobody can see it.

title: Read the RF site survey
instruction: Check the rooftop's emitters, the MPE boundary and which links are live.
rationale: A shared rooftop carries other tenants' antennas, most of them still live while you work. The survey is what says which of those are transmitting right now, where the exposure boundary actually sits in front of each one and who on the NOC has to sign off before this specific link comes down.

title: Find the MPE boundary
instruction: Locate the RF notice and the marked boundary in front of the dish face.
rationale: The boundary marks where the field strength in front of the dish exceeds the maximum permissible exposure limit for an occupational worker under FCC 47 CFR 1.1310. It's painted and signed so 'stand clear of the beam' is a distance in metres the crew can check against the deck, not a feeling about how close feels too close.

title: Call the far end
instruction: Raise the far site on the radio and get the link scheduled down with the network operations centre.
rationale: The other end of a link is a radio at a site nobody on this roof can see or control. It comes down by a logged agreement with the network operations centre, not by an assumption that the far end is idle — because the only thing worse than a live beam is one that came down on a guess and got put back up on a schedule nobody here knew about.

title: Key down and lock out the transmitter
instruction: Key the local transmitter down, open its breaker, then lock and tag it.
rationale: Keyed down is a software state, and software states come back on their own — a watchdog timer, a remote command, a firmware reset can all put the transmitter back on the air with nobody at this end touching anything. The breaker and the lock are what actually remove the power the software would need to do that while you're standing in front of the dish.

title: Set up for the parapet
instruction: Clip the lanyard to the certified roof anchor, check the harness, tether every tool.
rationale: The dish sits right at the parapet, which means every task on it happens at the edge of a fall. The anchor holds the technician, the tether holds every tool and every piece of hardware, and the pavement below this particular roof is a public sidewalk — anything dropped from here lands where people are walking.

title: Inspect the mount and radome
instruction: Look over the whole assembly and click the storm damage you find.
rationale: A link that drifted in a storm did not drift on its own — something on the mount or the radome gave way and let the wind move it. That damage is found and recorded before the alignment starts, because a fresh alignment on a cracked mount or a torn radome just walks off again in the next wind that comes through.

title: Free the azimuth clamp
instruction: Back the azimuth clamp off far enough for the dish to swing under hand pressure.
rationale: The clamp is what holds a couple of square feet of dish face steady against wind load, and it is loosened rather than removed for exactly that reason — even mid-adjustment, the dish stays held enough to stop it running away and swinging on the mast the moment a gust catches the face.

title: Pan onto the far site
instruction: Sweep the dish slowly across the far site's bearing — steady, no jerks.
rationale: A backhaul beam is a couple of degrees wide. Sweeping slowly is the only way to find the main lobe instead of locking onto a side lobe that will drop the link in the first rain.

title: Set the elevation
instruction: Walk the tilt through the peak and commit at the highest receive level.
rationale: Elevation is the other half of aiming the beam, and the true peak is one specific point across two axes at once — pan and tilt together, not either one alone. The eye can't judge a couple of degrees of elevation on a dish this size; the number climbing on the receive-level meter is the only honest way to know the peak has actually been found.

title: Confirm the receive level
instruction: With the far end on the test carrier, commit when the receive level is inside the design figure.
rationale: The design receive level is the number this path was engineered around, with a margin built in specifically for weather. A link accepted three decibels low still works fine on a clear day and drops out in exactly the rain fade the fade margin existed to survive, so an underpowered path fails the day it's actually needed.

title: Torque, weatherproof and hand back
instruction: Torque the azimuth and elevation clamps to spec, re-tape the connectors, then hand the path back to the operations centre.
rationale: The alignment just proven on the meter lasts exactly as long as the clamp torque holding it and the weatherproofing keeping water out of the connectors — loose either one and the path drifts or corrodes out from under a peak that was perfect an hour ago. The hand-back is the one thing that tells the network this link is carrying live traffic again.

situation: The radio keys up mid-sweep — NOC wants a live confirmation that the far end is still down before you swing the dish any closer to its old bearing.
instruction: NOC's calling for a lockout confirmation.
missed: The call went unanswered and the sweep continued across the beam's centreline on a lockout that was three steps old. NOC logged the ticket unconfirmed, and the far end could just as easily have been re-keyed by a second crew working the same site that morning.

situation: A gust catches you leaning into the sweep and the lanyard snaps taut — you've drifted further from the anchor than you meant to.
instruction: You've drifted off your anchor line.
missed: The drift went unnoticed through the rest of the sweep, well past the radius the anchor was rated to catch cleanly. Nothing happened this time, which is exactly how a rooftop crew stops checking the one thing that was never actually tested.

explanation: You went up with loose tools and hardware in an open pouch. Anything dropped from a roof is lethal on the pavement below; tools are tethered and hardware is in a closed container before the ladder.

You opened the waveguide flange with the transmitter still keyed. Opening a pressurised, energised waveguide sprays the dry air charge and puts the full transmit power out of an open flange at head height.

You stepped in front of a live microwave feed. At the dish face a backhaul link is far above the maximum permissible exposure limit; the injury is thermal, it is to the eyes and skin, and there is nothing to feel until the damage is done.
You worked at the parapet with no anchor. A rooftop edge is a fall hazard at any height, and a dish that swings while you are leaning on it takes your balance with it.

title: Read the ticket and circuit ID
instruction: Confirm the circuit, the port, and that the shutdown window is approved.
rationale: One strand in that tray is a hospital's imaging link and another is the backhaul for half the traffic signals north of the river. The ticket is what says which of the twelve is yours, which port feeds it, and which four hours the carrier has agreed you may break it in. Cutting the wrong strand is not a splice error — it is an outage somebody else has to explain.

title: Unlock and open the node cabinet
instruction: Turn the latch and swing the door back onto its stop, clear of the footway.
rationale: The door goes back against its stop and stays there. A street cabinet door loose in the wind takes the splicer's head or a passer-by's, and keeping the work off the footway is the part of OSHA's telecommunications standard that applies before any of the fibre content does. It is opened once, worked from, and shut — not propped half open for an hour.

title: Shut down the transmitter
instruction: Disable the OLT port feeding this strand at the shelf.
rationale: You make the strand dark at the source, on the shelf in front of you, not at the far end where you cannot see who else has their hands in the rack. A 1550 nm carrier is outside the visible band and the blink reflex never fires for it, which is why the ANSI Z136 guidance for fibre communication systems is built around the strand being proven dark before an end face is ever exposed.

title: Tag the port out
instruction: Take the tag-out card off the bench and hang it on the port you just disabled.
rationale: A disabled port with nothing hanging on it is a port the network operations centre re-enables the moment a customer rings about the service you just took down. The tag carries your name and your window, and in a cabinet nobody else is standing in it is the only thing that speaks for you to somebody two hundred miles away looking at the same alarm.

title: Prove the fibre is dark
instruction: Meter the strand and commit when the received power is safely dark.
rationale: Dark is a number in dBm, not an opinion. You shut one end down; the strand still runs miles to a node where a second technician may be doing exactly what you are doing, and the meter is the only thing that proves no light is arriving from their end. Anything above the threshold on the ticket means the end face stays capped until you know where the light is coming from.

title: Put on the laser eyewear
instruction: Take the wavelength-rated glasses from the case.
rationale: Rated for the wavelengths carried in this node, not the safety glasses out of the van door. They are not there for the strand you have just proven dark — they are there for the port somebody else brings back up while your eye is six inches from an open tray, which is the only way anybody has ever been hurt by a fibre.

title: Open the splice tray
instruction: Unclip the tray and bring it out flat before you route anything to the bench.
rationale: Trays come out one at a time and they come out flat. Every other strand in there is a live service belonging to somebody who has not been told anything is happening tonight, and a fibre levered against the edge of a tray takes a bend it never recovers from. That loss turns up weeks later as a link that fails on the cold nights and comes back by lunchtime.

title: Read the tray before you touch it
instruction: Three things in this tray are already wrong. Find them by looking.
rationale: Whatever is wrong in a tray gets blamed on the last technician who opened it, and more to the point it is the thing that fails next. A bend inside the minimum radius, a sleeve out of its holder and a strand with no slack all pass a glance and fail a winter, and every one of them is cheaper to put right now, with the tray already open and the truck already here.

title: Sleeve on first, then strip and clean
instruction: Thread the protection sleeve onto the strand, then strip the coating, then clean the bare fibre.
rationale: The sleeve goes on before anything else, because there is no way to thread it over a finished joint — forget it and the only remedy is to cut out the splice you just made and prepare both ends again. Then a clean strip with no nick in the cladding, then lint-free and solvent, because contamination is the largest single cause of a high-loss splice and both the cleaver and the arc assume a surface nothing has touched.

title: Cleave to angle
instruction: Set the cleaver and commit inside the acceptable cleave angle.
rationale: The end face has to be square to the axis of the core. Half a degree of angle and the two cores meet across a wedge of air instead of face to face; the arc fuses them anyway, the splicer reports a tidy-looking joint, and the loss stays in that link for the life of the cable. No amount of arc power recovers a bad cleave, so it gets a fresh blade position rather than one more go.

title: Fusion splice the joint
instruction: Load both ends, align and fire the arc.
rationale: The splicer aligns the cores, burns off what is left on the faces and fuses the glass, and it will do that just as confidently to a dirty fibre with a two-degree cleave as to a good one. Everything you control happened before this button; the estimate it puts on the screen afterwards measures your preparation, not the machine.

title: Verify the splice loss
instruction: Shoot the OTDR and commit when the splice loss is inside budget.
rationale: Every joint in the link spends part of a loss budget that was set when the route was designed, and that budget is what decides whether the far end still has enough light in three years, after the cable has been dug up and re-jointed twice by somebody else. A joint outside budget is cut out and redone now, while the tray is open and the window is still yours.

title: Run the full oven cycle on the sleeve
instruction: Slide the sleeve over the joint and hold it in the oven for the whole cycle.
rationale: That sleeve is the only mechanical strength a fusion splice has — the glass is butt-welded and snaps at the joint the first time anything pulls on it. A cycle cut short leaves the shrink incomplete and the strength member loose inside, which survives the bench, survives the tray, and lets go on the first hot afternoon the cabinet has.

title: Label and document
instruction: Label the strand, record the loss and restore the port.
rationale: The record is what the next technician trusts at three in the morning with no light in the cabinet and a customer on the phone: strand, port, measured loss, date, your name. Then the port comes back up and the tag comes off, in that order, because a service restored before it is written down is a service nobody can find again when it fails.

situation: P3 has come back up on the OLT shelf. Provisioning has re-enabled the port you shut down, and the strand lying open on the bench is live again.
instruction: You made it dark at the source. Go and make it dark again.
missed: You cleaved and spliced a strand that had gone live behind you. If your face was over the tray when that port came up — and it was, that is where the work happens — the retinal burn is done before anything at all tells you the light is there.

situation: The tray stack you propped open has settled. Tray 3 has dropped on its hinge and the strands routed out of it are pulling tight across the lip.
instruction: Your strand is not the only one in that tray.
missed: The tray hung on its own strands for the rest of the job. Nothing failed while you were standing there, which is exactly the problem — the bends went into live fibres and the trouble ticket lands months from now, on a circuit nobody has touched since tonight.

explanation: Isopropyl beside a running heat oven. The cleaning solvent is flammable and the oven cycles to 200 °C — one goes away before the other is switched on.
You looked into the fibre end. Transmission wavelengths are invisible and your blink reflex never fires — the retinal burn is done before you know the port was live.
Those are cleaved fibre offcuts on the bench. Bare glass shards work into skin and cannot be seen on an X-ray. They go in the sharps tube, immediately, every time.

That is the -48 V battery plant, not a fibre shelf. Telecom DC power will put thousands of amps into a dropped spanner without tripping anything, and the arc takes the tool, the busbar and the hand holding it. Nothing in that shelf is part of a splice — it is worked on isolated, by the power technician, under NFPA 70E.
That port has no label and no lockout. Working an unidentified port means the service you take down belongs to somebody who did not know it was coming.

title: Read the climb permit
instruction: Confirm the structure, the work height and which antennas nearby are live.
rationale: The permit names every transmitter that can reach this structure, including the ones on other owners' mounts that nobody at your company can switch off. You plan the RF survey and the climb route from that list before a single boot touches the first rung, because at height there is no way to find out what is radiating except by standing in it.

title: Survey the RF field at the work height
instruction: Read the RF survey meter and commit only inside the safe exposure band.
rationale: RF exposure is invisible, has no immediate sensation, and is averaged over time — so it is measured, not judged. Field strength climbs steeply as you close on a radiating panel, which is why the survey has to be taken at the work height rather than the ground, against the ANSI/IEEE-based maximum permissible exposure on the permit.

title: Lock out the transmitters
instruction: Confirm with the station engineer and lock the transmitter feed for antennas at your work height.
rationale: A verbal 'it's off' is not lockout. OSHA's control-of-hazardous-energy rule at 29 CFR 1910.147 wants a physical lock that only its owner can remove, and the IBEW engineer at the transmitter is the person who hangs it — because a broadcast chain has automatic restart logic that will bring a carrier back up on its own schedule, not yours.

title: Brief the rescue plan
instruction: Review the self-rescue kit, the descent route and who calls it if something goes wrong.
rationale: Hanging motionless in a harness pools blood in the legs and can put a conscious climber in trouble inside ten to twenty minutes, so a rescue has to be starting while the ground crew are still calling it in. OSHA expects prompt rescue to be planned, not improvised — and a plan first heard about while somebody is already suspended is not one.

title: Don the fall-arrest gear
instruction: Fit the harness, then clip lanyard 1, then clip lanyard 2.
rationale: The harness is fitted and checked first, because a lanyard clipped to slack webbing is a fall arrested by your ribs. Two lanyards is what makes one hundred percent tie-off physically possible at all — one stays anchored while the other reaches — and ANSI Z359 is why both of them are inspected by the wearer before every use, not annually.

title: Tether every tool
instruction: Clip a tool lanyard to each hand tool before you leave the ground.
rationale: Anything untethered is a dropped object the moment a glove slips, a hand cramps or a gust hits. Tethering is a ground task because it is the one place you can do it with both hands free and nothing below you — there is no safe way to fit a tool lanyard while standing on grating eighty feet above your own crew.

title: Walk the structure inspection
instruction: Check the guy wires, step bolts and anchors. Three things are wrong — find them by looking.
rationale: A guyed mast stands up because its guys are in tension; the ANSI/TIA-322 loading criteria the structure was designed to assume every strand is there and every anchor is sound. Weather and corrosion do not wait for the annual inspection, so the pre-climb walk is a search, not an assumption that yesterday's tower is today's tower.

title: Climb, maintaining 100% tie-off
instruction: Transfer your lanyards from anchor to anchor, low to high, never both unclipped at once.
rationale: One lanyard stays connected while the other reaches for the next anchor, and the overlap between them is the entire concept of one hundred percent tie-off. Taken out of order it stops being an overlap: skipping an anchor leaves a stretch of climb where the only thing holding you is the anchor you are already past.

title: Replace the antenna mounting bracket
instruction: Fit the new bracket and run the mount bolts down to torque with the tethered wrench.
rationale: The repair only happens once every control ahead of it is in place — locked-out RF, inspected structure, tied-off climber. Then it is a torque job: a mount bolt left finger-tight will back itself out under the wind loading ANSI/TIA-322 assumes this structure sees, and the panel it is holding is the next dropped object.

title: Recover and stow tools
instruction: Account for every tethered tool and stow them before descent.
rationale: The count at height has to match the count the ground crew wrote down before you left. Anything unaccounted for is either in the bag or lying on the grating waiting for the next gust, and a tower nobody can see the top of gives you no second chance to check — so the count happens before the descent, not after it.

title: Make a controlled descent
instruction: Engage the descent device and hold a steady brake the whole way down.
rationale: A descent device controls a fall by friction, and the friction only exists while the brake hand is loading the line — the device does nothing on its own. Eighty feet is long enough for a released brake to build speed no hand can take back, so the hold is the skill: steady, the whole way, without hurrying the last twenty feet.

title: Clear the RF lockout
instruction: Confirm the whole crew is off the structure, then release the transmitter lock with the station engineer.
rationale: The lock comes off last, by the person who put it on, once every climber has personally confirmed clear of the structure — a headcount, not an assumption that the last person down was the last person up. Restoring a carrier with somebody still on the mast is precisely the event the lockout existed to prevent.

situation: The wrench you set down on the grating has worked its way to the edge of the platform. Your ground crew is directly below.
instruction: Get it tethered before it goes over.
missed: The wrench went off the platform. A hard hat is rated for a two-kilogram object dropped two metres; this was neither. The ground crew never heard it coming, because it arrives before the sound does.

situation: Your ground crew has wandered in under the mast to look at the guy anchor — into the drop zone — and you are still on the platform.
instruction: Nobody stands under a climber.
missed: They stayed under the mast for the rest of the descent. Nothing fell this time, which is the only reason this is a note and not an incident report — the exposure was identical either way.

explanation: That lanyard's webbing is frayed clean through the outer sheath. The ANSI Z359 fall protection standards retire a shock-absorbing lanyard after a single arrest event and on any sign of damage, because torn webbing can part well below the 5,000 lb the system is supposed to be good for.

That antenna panel is still transmitting. RF at this range heats tissue from the inside with no sensation to warn you until after the exposure, and stray current will arc into an ungrounded tool the instant it touches the feed line. The permit's 2.5 mW/cm² figure is the ANSI/IEEE-derived exposure limit the FCC enforces.

That wrench is sitting untethered on the platform grating. Eighty feet of fall puts a two-pound wrench on the ground at over forty miles an hour, and a hard hat is tested against a fraction of that energy — dropped objects are consistently among the leading causes of death in tower work.

That beam is past your last clipped point. Moving to it before the second lanyard is engaged leaves you attached to nothing for the length of the transfer, and the transfer is where climbers fall — which is the whole reason OSHA and every NATE climber programme say one hundred percent, not ninety-nine.

title: Read the alarm
instruction: Read the building management panel: which unit, which alarm, and since when.
rationale: A high-temperature alarm, a fan failure and a filter alarm send the technician to different places with different urgency; reading the panel first puts the right tool in hand and the right unit in front of you instead of chasing the loudest noise in the hall.

title: Tell the hall operator
instruction: Radio the hall operator: the unit, the alarm, and that you are responding.
rationale: The hall operator sees the whole hall's cooling and load and may already be moving work off the affected racks; telling them first means two people are working the same problem with the same facts.

title: Read the supply air against its band
instruction: Bring the supply-air reading up to where it is and commit — inside the hall's band or not?
rationale: The supply air leaving the unit says whether it is still cooling at all, and the hall's operating procedure sets the band; read against that written band, the reading decides whether this is a service call or a race to bring the standby unit on.

title: Walk the unit down
instruction: Check the filter differential, then the fan status, then the condensate pan.
rationale: A walk-down in the same order every time finds the common causes — a loaded filter, a stopped fan, a full pan — without opening anything, and tells the technician what to bring for the repair before the unit is isolated.

title: Find why the unit is failing
instruction: Find what is causing the alarm on the unit.
rationale: Knowing the cause decides the repair and whether it is safe to restore: a clogged filter is a swap, while a tripped fan breaker is a fault somebody has to find before the fan runs again.

title: Bring the standby unit on
instruction: Start the standby unit per the hall's procedure and confirm it is running.
rationale: The hall's racks cannot wait for the repair, so the redundancy the hall was built with is brought on first; confirming the standby is actually running and moving air, not just switched, is what lets the failed unit be taken out of service.

title: Watch the hall recover
instruction: Keep watching the cold-aisle reading as the standby unit takes the load.
rationale: A standby unit that starts but does not bring the cold aisle back is a second problem; watching the reading recover proves the hall is held before anyone isolates the failed unit and takes away what is left of its cooling.

title: Isolate the failed unit
instruction: Open the unit's disconnect, apply your lock, then hang your tag.
rationale: The unit's fans and heaters restart on their own controls, and the building management system can call it back on; the disconnect, your lock and your tag are what keep it off while hands are inside.

title: Test the unit dead
instruction: Hold the proven tester on each phase at the unit's terminals until it reads absent.
rationale: A unit can be fed from more than one source, and an open disconnect can be the wrong one; the test at the unit's own terminals, with a tester proven before and after, is the proof that what you are about to touch is dead.

title: Open the access panel
instruction: Turn the access-panel latch and swing the panel open.
rationale: The panel comes off only once the unit is proven dead, and it is swung open on its hinge rather than lifted off so it does not fall into the aisle or onto a floor tile edge.

title: Fit the new filters
instruction: Carry the new filter bank to the slot and seat it with the airflow arrow the right way.
rationale: A filter fitted backwards or not seated in its frame lets air bypass it, and the unit's coil loads with dust instead; the arrow and the frame are checked because that is what makes the swap a repair.

title: Log the response
instruction: Log the alarm, the cause, the standby start and the lockout, and tell the hall operator the unit's state.
rationale: The log is how the next shift knows the hall is running on its standby unit and why, and the tripped breaker stays on it as an open item until someone has found what tripped it.

situation: The clean-agent suppression panel at the hall door has gone to pre-alarm on a detector in this zone.
instruction: Go to the suppression panel and read the zone and the state.
missed: The pre-alarm went unread while the work went on, so nobody in the hall knew which zone had tripped or what the plan said to do next.

situation: Condensate from the unit's pan is running across the floor toward a power whip at the end of the row.
instruction: Get the spill kit down across the water's path.
missed: The water reached the power whip with nothing in its way, putting a slip and an electrical hazard in the same spot.

explanation: You went to prop the cold-aisle containment door open to let the heat out. Containment works by keeping hot and cold air apart; propped open, it mixes them and makes every rack in the row run hotter.
You went to open the fan section with the unit still energised. The fans restart on their own control, and a hand in a fan section when they do is the injury the lockout exists to prevent.

You went to reset the unit's tripped breaker again and again. A breaker that trips is reporting a fault, and resetting it onto that fault repeatedly can turn a failed fan motor into an arc in the panel.
You went to silence the alarm and walk on. A silenced alarm is still a failing unit, and in a live hall the racks on its side warm with every minute nobody is working the problem.

title: Read the drawings and the installation instructions
instruction: Read the busway drawings and the manufacturer's instructions: the run, the joint torque and the test called for.
rationale: The torque value, the joint sequence and the test voltage all belong to this manufacturer's product, and they live in its instructions; working from another product's numbers is how a joint ends up under- or over-torqued with a clean conscience.

title: Isolate the run upstream
instruction: Open the upstream breaker that feeds the run, apply your lock, then hang your tag.
rationale: The busway is fed from a switchboard in another room, so the only protection for the crew on the lift is a lock on that breaker they hold themselves; the tag tells whoever is at the switchboard which run is being worked and by whom.

title: Prove the run dead
instruction: Prove the tester on a known source, test the bars at the open end, then prove the tester again — commit when it reads absent.
rationale: The drawings can name the wrong breaker and a switchboard can be mislabelled; the test on the bars themselves, with a tester proven before and after, is what makes this run an electrically safe work condition rather than a hopeful one.

title: Pre-use the scissor lift
instruction: Check the guardrails and their pins, then test the ground and platform controls, emergency lowering included.
rationale: The guardrails are the fall protection on a scissor lift and the controls are how it comes down if something goes wrong; both are proven on the floor, where a loose pin or a dead emergency-lowering valve is a tag-out rather than a rescue.

title: Close the lift gate
instruction: Step in and close the lift's entry gate behind you.
rationale: The entry gate is a section of the guardrail, and it only protects when it is shut; closing it before the platform moves is the habit that keeps it from being open at height.

title: Raise the lift to the busway
instruction: Hold the raise control and bring the platform up steadily below the hangers, watching overhead.
rationale: A scissor lift raised smoothly, with an eye overhead, stops short of trays, sprinkler pipe and the busway itself; raised in bursts while looking down at the controls, it pins a hand or a head against the ceiling services.

title: Hang the busway section
instruction: Bring the section to its hangers and seat it on both before letting go.
rationale: A busway section is heavy and long, and seated on one hanger it pivots; seating both ends before releasing it keeps the weight on the hangers and off the joint that has not been made yet.

title: Inspect the joint before it is made
instruction: Look into the joint before it is closed and find what has to be put right.
rationale: A joint made up over a cracked insulator or a flake of swarf looks exactly like a good one once the cover is on, and both fail under load as heat. The only chance to see them is before the bolt is torqued.

title: Torque the joint bolt
instruction: Turn the calibrated torque wrench on the joint bolt until it clicks at the manufacturer's value.
rationale: The joint bolt sets the pressure between the bars, and the manufacturer's value is the pressure that carries the rated current without overheating or cracking the insulators; a calibrated wrench is the only tool that knows when it has got there.

title: Mark and verify every joint
instruction: Mark the torqued bolt and check every joint on the run carries its mark.
rationale: The torque mark is field evidence that the bolt was taken to its value, and a check along the whole run catches the joint that was hand-tightened at the end of a shift and never went back to. The sign-off relies on every mark being there.

title: Insulation-resistance test the run
instruction: Hold the insulation-resistance test steady on each bar for the full test time.
rationale: An insulation-resistance test at the manufacturer's test voltage finds damaged insulators, moisture and debris across the whole run before it is energised; held for the full time, the reading means something, while a flick of the test button measures only how fast the needle moved.

title: Sign off the torque and the test
instruction: Sign the sheet: each joint, the wrench's calibration number and the test result.
rationale: The sign-off ties every joint to the wrench that torqued it and the test that proved it, so if a joint ever runs hot the record shows who, with what, and against which value — and whether the wrench was in calibration that day.

situation: A labourer is pushing a pallet jack of cable reels straight under the raised lift's platform.
instruction: Sound the lift horn and stop them before they are under you.
missed: The pallet jack went under the lift with nobody stopping it, putting a person right where anything dropped from the platform lands.

situation: The commissioning agent is calling — the adjacent busway run is about to be energised for testing.
instruction: Answer on the site radio and confirm where your crew and your lockout are.
missed: The call went unanswered while the next run was energised beside the crew, with nobody confirming whose lock was on which breaker.

explanation: You went to stand on the lift's mid-rail to reach the hanger. Standing on the rail puts your centre of gravity above the guardrail that was meant to stop you, which turns the lift's fall protection into a lever.
You went to raise the lift with its entry gate open. The guardrails are the fall protection on a scissor lift, and an open gate is a missing section of guardrail at the height of the busway.

You went to run the joint bolt up with an impact gun and call it tight. A busway joint's bolt is torqued to the manufacturer's value with a calibrated wrench because under-torque overheats the joint and over-torque cracks the insulators — neither shows by feel.

You went to open the joint cover with the run still fed from upstream. A busway carries the hall's load in bare bars inside that housing, and a joint opened live is an arc-flash source at arm's length on a lift with nowhere to step back to.

title: Read the lift plan and the dive plan
instruction: Read the lift plan and the dive plan: the pod's weight per the plan, the crane's radius, the sea-state limit and the diving limits.
rationale: The lift plan fixes what the crane may lift at what radius and in what sea, and the dive plan fixes what the diver does and when they are out; both are read before the hook goes in the water so the day's decisions are made against paper rather than against impatience.

title: Read the sea state against the lift plan
instruction: Bring the sea-state reading up to where it is and commit — inside the lift plan's limit or not?
rationale: A crane on a boat lifts a load that moves with the swell, and the lift plan's sea-state limit is where that motion stays within what the crane and the crew can control; read against the written limit, the reading is the go or no-go for the whole recovery.

title: Prepare the deck
instruction: Clear and chock the deck cradle, then flake out the tag lines and man them.
rationale: The pod needs somewhere to land the moment it clears the rail, and the tag lines need hands on them before it gets there; a deck prepared in advance keeps the load's time in the air as short as it can be.

title: Confirm the diver is out
instruction: Confirm with the dive supervisor that the diver who rigged the bridle is out of the water and accounted for.
rationale: The diver rigged the bridle on the seabed skid and the lift must not start until they are back on deck; the dive supervisor, who has been tending them, is the one person who can say so, and the lift waits for that word every time.

title: Check the deck-end rigging
instruction: Check the crane's hook, shackle and sling before the hoist and find what stops the lift.
rationale: The rigging at the hook end is what the crew can see and check from deck, and a pin that can back out or a sling leg with a kink fails under exactly the swinging, snatching load a recovery at sea produces.

title: Hoist the pod slowly off the bottom
instruction: Hold the hoist control and bring the pod up slowly off its skid and through the splash zone.
rationale: Breaking a pod out of the seabed and bringing it through the surface are the moments the load on the crane changes fastest; a slow, steady hoist lets the crane operator feel it and stop before a snatch load reaches the boom.

title: Control the pod over the rail
instruction: Keep the pod steady on the tag lines as it comes up over the rail and in over the deck.
rationale: Over the rail the pod swings with the roll, and the tag lines, worked from outside its landing area, are what keep it from striking the rail, the crane or the crew; steady control is continuous work until it is down.

title: Land the pod in its cradle
instruction: Guide the pod down into the deck cradle and land it square.
rationale: A pod landed square in its cradle sits on the supports it was designed for; landed on the roll or off-centre, it rocks, stresses its frame and can shift before it is fastened.

title: Sea-fasten, then release the hook
instruction: Chain the pod into its cradle, then slack and release the crane hook.
rationale: Until it is fastened the crane is still holding the pod on a moving deck; releasing the hook first leaves a heavy load free to shift with the next roll. Fastened, then released, the pod is never unrestrained.

title: Isolate the pod's cable
instruction: Open the shore-cable breaker named in the pod procedure, then apply your lock and tag.
rationale: The pod's cable is how power reaches the equipment behind the hatch, and a lock you hold on its breaker is what keeps it dead while the hatch is open; the tag names the pod and the person inside it.

title: Read the pod's leak lamp
instruction: Read the pod's leak-detect lamp and its status panel against the pod procedure before the hatch.
rationale: The leak lamp is the pod's own report of whether water or a changed atmosphere is inside; it is read on deck, before anyone opens the hatch, because the answer changes what happens next.

title: Open the hatch bolts in pattern
instruction: Turn the hatch bolts off in the pattern the pod procedure shows, easing the seal evenly.
rationale: A sealed hatch comes off evenly so its seal and faces are not damaged for the next deployment and any difference in pressure is released gradually round the whole seal, not through one side; the pattern is the pod procedure's for that reason.

title: Log the recovery
instruction: Log the recovery: the sea state, the lift, the lockout, the leak lamp reading and the hatch.
rationale: The recovery log ties the pod's condition on deck to the conditions it came up in, so the engineers reading it later know whether what they find inside came from the seabed or from the lift.

situation: A wake from a passing vessel is rolling the workboat and the pod is swinging on the hook just below the rail.
instruction: Stop the hoist at the crane's stop control until the boat settles.
missed: The hoist kept coming up through the roll with the pod swinging at the rail, where a roll puts it into the rail and the crew.

situation: The skipper is calling from the wheelhouse — a squall line is coming down the channel toward the boat.
instruction: Answer the bridge on the radio and agree whether the lift lands now or holds.
missed: The skipper's call went unanswered with the pod still on the hook, so the squall arrived before anyone had decided to land or hold.

explanation: You went to put a hand on the pod between it and the rail to steady it. A roll of the boat closes that gap faster than a hand can come out; the tag line is how a load is steadied from a distance.

You went to start the hoist with the diver still in the water. A load coming off the seabed stirs the bottom, swings on its bridle and can foul the diver's umbilical — the lift waits until the dive supervisor says the diver is out.
You went to unbolt the hatch with the shore cable still energised. The pod's power and its batteries are behind that hatch, and the cable is isolated and locked before anyone reaches in.
You went to stand under the pod as it swung in over the deck. A suspended load moves with the boat as well as the crane, and the only safe place for a person is outside the area it could land in.

title: Read the work ticket and the floor plan
instruction: Read the ticket: which tile, which tray, the cable to lay and the hall's rules for an open tile.
rationale: A floor plan says which tile opens over which tray and what else runs in the plenum there — power whips, chilled-water pipe, fire detection — so the tile that comes up is the right one and nothing under it is a surprise.

title: Tell the hall operator before a tile comes up
instruction: Call the hall operator: which tile is coming up, for how long, and who is attending it.
rationale: In a live hall the raised floor is also the cooling plenum, and the operator is watching its pressure and the rack temperatures; telling them first means a change in the readings has an explanation and a person to call.

title: Barricade the tile before it comes up
instruction: Set the cones round the tile, then hang the barrier chain.
rationale: The barricade goes up before the opening exists, so there is never a moment when the hole is there and the warning is not; an aisle is a route people walk while reading labels, not the floor.

title: Prove the lifter's vacuum
instruction: Pump the suction lifter onto the tile and commit when its gauge reads in the green.
rationale: A suction cup can feel firm while it bleeds air through a nicked seal, and a tile that drops from a lifter lands on a foot or into the plenum on a cable; the gauge reads the vacuum the cups are actually holding, which is what the lift depends on.

title: Lift the tile straight up
instruction: Hold the lifter and bring the tile straight up and out, keeping it level.
rationale: A tile lifted straight and level clears its neighbours' edges without prising them up, and does not swing into the rack or the person beside you; tilted out, it drags a corner across the stringer and the next tile along.

title: Set the tile down out of the aisle
instruction: Carry the tile to its rest spot against the rack end, out of the walkway.
rationale: A loose tile left in the aisle is a second trip hazard next to the first, and a tile leaning where a cart can catch it falls; set against the rack end it is out of the walkway and ready to go back.

title: Inspect the plenum under the tile
instruction: Look under the floor and find what needs putting right before the tile goes back.
rationale: The open tile is the only time anyone sees this part of the plenum, so it is looked at, not just reached into: a loose pedestal head makes a rocking tile and a crushed cable is a failure waiting in the tray.

title: Lay the cable into the tray
instruction: Check the tray's bonding jumper is in place, then lay the cable into the tray and tie it — never drag it over the side rail.
rationale: A metal tray is bonded so a fault finds a path to ground instead of a person, and a broken jumper is found by looking; the cable is laid in by hand because a cable dragged over a rail is crushed at the rail and its performance or insulation suffers there.

title: Watch the cold aisle while the tile is out
instruction: Keep watching the cold-aisle reading beside the opening while you work.
rationale: An open tile vents the plenum where it should not and starves the perforated tiles in front of the racks, so the cold-aisle reading beside the opening is watched for as long as it is open — the job is quick because the hall is live.

title: Reseat the tile square
instruction: Turn the tile square to the grid and lower it onto its pedestals until it sits flush.
rationale: A tile set down out of square rides up on a stringer and rocks, and a rocking tile under a cart wheel is how the next opening appears; turned square and lowered, it seats on all four pedestals at once.

title: Walk the tile
instruction: Step on each corner of the reseated tile and check it is flush and does not rock.
rationale: The last check is the one the next person does without thinking — walking on it; a corner that dips under a boot now is fixed now, before it dips under a loaded cart.

title: Close out the ticket
instruction: Close the ticket: the cable laid, the findings under the floor and the tile back, and tell the hall operator.
rationale: The close-out tells the hall operator the plenum is sealed again and records what was found underneath, so a loose pedestal or a crushed cable becomes somebody's job rather than a memory.

situation: Someone is pushing a loaded server cart down the aisle toward the open tile, looking at the rack labels, not the floor.
instruction: Hold up the stop paddle and stop the cart before the barricade.
missed: The cart kept coming toward the opening with nobody stopping it, and a loaded wheel at the edge of an open tile drops into the plenum.

situation: The rack next to the opening has raised an inlet temperature alarm — the open tile is starving its perforated tile of cold air.
instruction: Call the hall operator on the phone and tell them what is open and where.
missed: The alarm went unreported while the rack inlet heated, and the hall operator had no idea an open tile was the reason.

explanation: You went to drag the cable over the tray's side rail. A cable pulled over an edge is crushed and its jacket scraped at that point, and the damage hides under the floor until the link fails or the power cable beside it heats.
You went to leave the open tile to fetch more cable. An opening in a live hall's aisle, even barricaded, is attended by the person who opened it until the tile is back.

You went to lift the next tile along while the first was still out. Two adjacent tiles out take away the support the grid's stringers rely on and can let the floor around the opening shift — the floor manufacturer limits it for a reason.

You went to step across the open tile space to reach the rack. An open tile is a hole to the slab below, edged by tiles that can tip when a boot lands on their edge — the way round is along the barricade.
